entry.title: The harbour at low tide
entry.content:
• Camera: 6x7 rangefinder, 80mm
  • Film: Tri-X, developed in the studio
  • Prints: silver gelatin, 50 x 60 cm
  • Book: Tidewater Press, 2026

Twice a day the water leaves, and the harbour shows you its bones: the chains, the old tyres hung as fenders, the steps worn into a bowl by two hundred years of boots. For six winters I stood at the same wall at the lowest water of each month and made one exposure.

January. The outer harbour, fog lifting at eleven.

February. The boy who sells bait, walking out to the second mooring post.

What the mud keeps

A spoon, a bicycle bell, the brass plate from a boat that sank before anyone now living was born. The mud keeps everything and gives it back slowly.

The harbour is not a place. It is a schedule that happens to have walls.

March. The old pier at dusk, the last frame on the roll.

The book collects forty-eight of these plates, one for each month, in the order they were made.
entry.summary: Six winters at the same harbour wall, photographed at the lowest water of each month.

entry.title: Fog studies
entry.content:
Nine mornings this winter the fog came in before seven. Each time I walked to the end of the breakwater and photographed whatever was on the water.

The pilot boat, second morning.

Ninth morning. No boat at all.
entry.summary: A boat, a mast and the horizon, on the nine mornings this winter when the fog came in.

entry.title: Lamps on the breakwater
entry.content:
Seven lamps run along the breakwater. Through the darkest week of the year I made one four-minute exposure of each, from the same spot on the slipway.

Four minutes at f/16, the third night.
entry.summary: Seven lamps, one long exposure each, through the darkest week of the year.

entry.title: Keeping a commonplace book
entry.content:
A commonplace book is a notebook of things worth keeping: quotations, sums, recipes, the name of a bolt. I have kept one for nineteen years.1 This is how it works, in more detail than anyone needs.

The rules

  1. Write the date before anything else.
  2. Copy quotations by hand, with the page number.
  3. Never tear out a page; cross it out instead.
  4. Index the book when it is full, not before.

Paper - a plain A5 notebook with numbered pages.

Pen - whatever is in the coat pocket.

Index - the last four pages, alphabetical, by subject.

A worked example

Here is the index format I settled on after many bad ones:

Subject Pages Notes
Tides 4, 17, 52 tables copied from the harbour office
Radios 9, 10 valve numbers, a wiring sketch
Bread 33 a recipe from a neighbour

When the book moved to a computer I wrote a tiny script to rebuild the index:

import re

def index(lines):
    entries = {}
    for page, line in lines:
        for tag in re.findall(r"#(\w+)", line):
            entries.setdefault(tag, []).append(page)
    return dict(sorted(entries.items()))

The script lives in the back of the book too, written out by hand.2

Whatever you copy out, you keep twice: once on the page and once in the hand.

What it is for

Mostly it is for remembering where I read something. Sometimes it is for noticing that I have copied the same sentence three times in ten years, which tells me more about myself than any diary.

  1. The first one was a school exercise book with a broken spine. ↩

  2. Yes, this is a little absurd. ↩
entry.summary: A long note on the oldest writing tool I use, with the system that keeps it useful.

Six portraits of people who keep the fleet working, made over two weeks in the net loft and the boatyard.

Net loft, Thursday afternoon.

entry.title: Mast and weather
entry.content:
• Client: North Coast Sailing Club
  • Role: Director, director of photography
  • Format: Super 16, 9 minutes

The club asked for a film about one hundred years of racing. I made a film about one boat and one summer of weather instead, and they were kind about it.
entry.summary: A short film for the sailing club's centenary, shot on Super 16 over one summer.

entry.title: Night ferry
entry.content:
• Director: Rowan Vale
  • Cinematography: Rowan Vale
  • Sound: Ada Marsh
  • Running time: 14 minutes

The last ferry leaves at eleven and comes back empty. I rode it forty times with a camera and a sound recordist, and the crew stopped noticing us by the second week.
entry.summary: A fourteen-minute film made on the last ferry of the night, over one winter of crossings.

entry.title: Field recording at the pier
entry.content: We set up at seven on the end of the pier: two microphones, a folding chair and a flask. The recording runs for forty minutes. The gull arrives at minute twelve.
entry.summary: Notes from a sound day for Night Ferry: two microphones, a gull and a very patient audience.

entry.title: Shore line
entry.content: One stone, one tripod mark scratched into it, twenty-four spring tides.
